Intranasal steroid drops/spray (1st-line) + saline → short oral steroids → surgery (intranasal or endoscopic polypectomy) if fails.
Recurrence
Common (esp. AERD); aspirin desensitisation + biologics (dupilumab) for severe/recurrent disease.
ENT__Head & Neck Cancer:
Overview — head & neck cancer
Malignancies of the upper aerodigestive tract — larynx, oral cavity/tongue, nasopharynx and beyond — mostly squamous cell carcinoma, linked to smoking, alcohol and HPV/EBV.
The organising principle: recognise the red flags for 2-week-wait referral — persistent hoarseness (>3 weeks), a neck lump, a non-healing oral ulcer, dysphagia, or unilateral otalgia/nasal symptoms.
CancerClueRisk factor
Laryngeal cancer / hoarse voicepersistent hoarseness >3 weekssmoking/alcohol → refer + laryngoscopy
Oral cavity & tongue lesionsnon-healing ulcer / red-white patchsmoking, alcohol, betel → biopsy
Nasopharyngeal carcinomaunilateral nasal obstruction/epistaxis, neck node, adult OMEEBV; Southern Chinese
Head & neck cancer (red flags)hoarseness, neck lump, dysphagia, unilateral otalgia→ 2-week-wait
Persistent hoarseness >3 weeks, a neck lump, or a non-healing oral ulcer = urgent (2-week-wait) referral. Unilateral otitis media with effusion in an adult → exclude nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
What & Why

Laryngeal cancer is a malignancy of the larynx (voice box) — the commonest head & neck cancer, and >90% are squamous cell carcinomas (SCC) arising from the mucosal lining. It matters because it presents with a very common symptom — hoarseness — that is usually benign, so the examinable skill is knowing which hoarse voice is a red flag (and triggering an urgent cancer referral) versus the many benign causes. It’s strongly smoking- and alcohol-driven (largely preventable) and, when caught early (as glottic tumours often are, because they cause hoarseness early), it’s very treatable with voice preservation.

The core anatomy (why site matters): the larynx has three regions, and the site determines how early it presents and how it spreads.
🎯 Glottis (vocal cords) — commonest
  • Hoarseness appears EARLY (any cord lesion changes the voice) → often caught early
  • Poor lymphatic supply → spreads late (better prognosis)
Supraglottis / Subglottis
  • Supraglottis (above cords): presents later — sore throat, dysphagia, referred otalgia, neck lump; rich lymphatics → early nodal spread
  • Subglottis (below cords): rare, presents late with stridor/airway obstruction
The Decisive Fork — Is This Hoarse Voice a Red Flag?

Hoarseness (dysphonia) is the key symptom — most causes are benign, but you must screen for the sinister.

CategoryCauses
Benign / inflammatoryAcute laryngitis (viral/URTI — commonest), voice overuse/misuse (vocal cord nodules — “singer’s nodules”), vocal cord polyps
RefluxLaryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR)
NeurologicalRecurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (vocal cord palsy)
EndocrineHypothyroidism (vocal cord myxoedema)
Iatrogenic / otherInhaled steroids (candidiasis/myopathy), post-intubation, smoking
MalignantLaryngeal cancer (and lung/thyroid/oesophageal cancers via nerve involvement)
The rule: persistent hoarseness (>3 weeks), especially in a smoker/drinker over 45–50, is laryngeal cancer until proven otherwise → urgent referral.
Referral — NICE NG12 (2-Week-Wait)
Consider a suspected-cancer (2-week-wait) referral for laryngeal cancer in people aged 45 and over with: persistent unexplained hoarseness, OR an unexplained lump in the neck.

Also refer / urgently investigate: stridor → same-day; persistent sore throat/dysphagia, otalgia with a normal ear, haemoptysis, or an unexplained neck lump (cross-reference the NG12 head & neck criteria).

Risk Factors
  • Smoking — the dominant factor (~90–95% of patients smoke; strong dose-response)
  • Alcohol (excess — synergistic with smoking)
  • Male sex, older age (60–70)
  • HPV (especially supraglottic; more established in oropharyngeal cancer)
  • Occupational exposures (asbestos, wood dust), lower socioeconomic status, previous radiotherapy, GORD/LPR
Clinical Features
  • Persistent hoarseness / voice change (dysphonia) — the cardinal symptom (early in glottic cancer)
  • Persistent sore throat, dysphagia or odynophagia
  • Referred otalgia (ear pain with a normal ear) — via the vagus nerve
  • Unexplained neck lump (nodal metastasis — especially supraglottic)
  • Stridor / dyspnoea (airway narrowing — an emergency sign)
  • Haemoptysis, weight loss, chronic cough; a globus sensation (overlaps with LPR)
Investigations
  • Flexible nasendoscopy / laryngoscopy — the key first-line examination (visualises the larynx/vocal cords, assesses cord mobility + any lesion)
  • Biopsy under direct (micro)laryngoscopy — for histological diagnosis (usually general anaesthetic)
  • Imaging for staging: CT/MRI neck + thorax (local extent + nodes + chest); PET-CT in some
  • Assess airway and swallowing; MDT staging (TNM)
Management

Managed by the head & neck MDT.

  • Early-stage (T1/T2), especially glottic: radiotherapy or transoral laser microsurgery — aiming for voice/organ preservation (excellent local control, ~90%+ for early glottic)
  • Advanced disease: chemoradiotherapy (organ-preservation) or surgery — partial or total laryngectomy (total laryngectomy leaves a permanent tracheostomy/stoma + need for voice rehabilitation)
  • Neck dissection for nodal disease
  • Smoking & alcohol cessation — essential (continuing worsens outcomes + second-tumour risk)
  • Voice/swallow rehabilitation (SALT), MDT support
Two Key “Hoarse Voice” Conditions
🔥 Laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR)
  • GORD-type acid reflux reaching the larynx → inflammatory change to the laryngeal mucosa
  • Features: globus (lump-in-throat) — worse swallowing SALIVA, not food/drink; hoarseness, chronic cough, dysphagia, heartburn; posterior pharynx may look erythematous; exam otherwise normal (no mass)
  • Management: lifestyle measures, PPI, sodium alginate (Gaviscon)
  • LPR is a diagnosis of exclusion — persistent hoarseness still needs the larynx visualised to rule out cancer
🧠 Recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) palsy
  • The RLN (a branch of the vagus) supplies the intrinsic laryngeal muscles → damage → vocal cord palsy → hoarse/breathy voice
  • The left RLN loops under the aortic arch (longer course) → more often affected; causes: lung cancer (apex), thyroid cancer/surgery, aortic aneurysm, mediastinal disease
  • An unexplained vocal cord palsy warrants imaging of the whole nerve course (skull base → mediastinum) to find the cause
Exam Pearls
What it is
Commonest head & neck cancer; >90% SCC; strongly smoking + alcohol driven.
Site
Glottic (commonest): hoarseness EARLY, spreads late (good prognosis). Supraglottic: presents late (sore throat/dysphagia/otalgia/neck lump), early nodal spread. Subglottic: stridor.
2WW referral
NICE NG12: ≥45 with persistent unexplained hoarseness OR unexplained neck lump. (Stridor → same-day.)
Golden rule
Persistent hoarseness >3 weeks in a smoker/drinker = laryngeal cancer until proven otherwise.
Red flags
Referred otalgia (normal ear), neck lump, dysphagia, stridor, haemoptysis, weight loss.
Investigate
Nasendoscopy → microlaryngoscopy + biopsy → CT/MRI staging.
Treatment
Early glottic → radiotherapy / transoral laser (voice preservation); advanced → chemoradiotherapy or laryngectomy (+ stoma).
Hoarse differentials
Laryngitis, vocal nodules/polyps, LPR, RLN palsy, hypothyroidism, inhaled steroids, cancer.
LPR
Globus worse swallowing SALIVA, normal exam → PPI/Gaviscon — but exclude cancer first.
Left RLN palsy
Think lung/thyroid/mediastinal disease (loops under the aortic arch).
What & Why

Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a squamous cell carcinoma arising from the epithelium of the nasopharynx (the space behind the nose, above the soft palate). It stands apart from other head & neck cancers because it has a completely distinctive profile: strongly linked to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a striking geographic/ethnic distribution (endemic in Southern China / SE Asia), a younger age group, and it is highly radiosensitive (so radiotherapy, not surgery, is the mainstay). The examinable trap: it presents with vague, “innocent” ENT symptoms (a blocked ear, a nosebleed, a neck lump) that get dismissed → often diagnosed late.

The core anatomy: NPC classically arises in the fossa of Rosenmüller (a recess in the lateral nasopharyngeal wall). Its position explains the whole presentation: near the Eustachian tube (→ blocks it → unilateral middle-ear effusion), near the nasal cavity (→ obstruction/epistaxis), rich in lymphatics (→ early neck-node spread — often the first sign), and near the skull base/cranial nerves (→ cranial nerve palsies).
The Decisive Fork — What Makes NPC Different
Nasopharyngeal carcinomaTypical H&N SCC (larynx/oral)
Key causeEpstein-Barr virus (EBV)Smoking + alcohol
EpidemiologyEndemic: Southern China, SE Asia, N Africa, InuitWorldwide, smoking-related
AgeYounger (can affect 30s–50s)Older (60–70s)
HistologyOften non-keratinising / undifferentiated (EBV+)Keratinising SCC
First presentationOften a neck lump (nodal spread)Local symptoms (hoarseness etc.)
TreatmentRadiotherapy ± chemo (radiosensitive)Often surgery ± radiotherapy
Risk Factors
  • Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) — the major aetiological agent (raised EBV serology / EBV DNA)
  • Ethnicity/geography — Southern Chinese (Cantonese), Southeast Asian, North African, Inuit populations; risk persists in migrants
  • Diet — salt-preserved foods/salted fish (nitrosamines), especially in childhood
  • Genetic predisposition (HLA associations, family history)
  • Smoking, occupational exposures (formaldehyde, wood dust)
Clinical Features

The “innocent-looking” symptoms — often unilateral.

  • Neck lump (cervical lymphadenopathy) — the commonest presenting feature (often the first sign; upper/posterior cervical nodes)
  • Unilateral serous otitis media / middle-ear effusion — from Eustachian tube obstruction; a persistent unilateral middle-ear effusion in an adult is NPC until proven otherwise
  • Nasal symptoms — unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis, or blood-stained nasal discharge
  • Cranial nerve palsies — from skull-base invasion (e.g. diplopia (CN VI), facial numbness (CN V)) → often indicates advanced disease
  • Headache, otalgia, conductive hearing loss (from the effusion)
  • Trotter’s triad (classic): conductive deafness + ipsilateral facial/temporal pain (CN V3) + palatal palsy
Investigations
  • Nasendoscopy — visualise the nasopharynx / fossa of Rosenmüller
  • Biopsy — histological diagnosis (nasopharyngeal biopsy)
  • EBV markers — EBV serology / plasma EBV DNA (diagnosis, monitoring, and in some regions screening)
  • Imaging: MRI (nasopharynx/skull base — best for local extent) + CT; PET-CT for staging/distant disease
  • Assess the neck — an unexplained neck lump may prompt a 2WW head & neck referral, but avoid excisional lymph node biopsy of a neck node before the primary is found (find the primary first — FNA/core if needed)
Management

Managed by the head & neck MDT.

  • Radiotherapy is the mainstay — NPC is highly radiosensitive, and its location makes surgery difficult; intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) to the primary + neck
  • Concurrent chemoradiotherapy (+ platinum-based chemo) for locally advanced disease
  • Surgery has a limited role (mainly salvage for residual/recurrent nodal or local disease — e.g. neck dissection)
  • Distant metastasis (bone, lung, liver) → systemic chemotherapy ± immunotherapy
  • Prognosis depends heavily on stage; early disease has good outcomes, but late presentation is common; EBV DNA levels help monitor response/recurrence
Exam Pearls
What it is
SCC of the nasopharynx (fossa of Rosenmüller); the “different” head & neck cancer — EBV-linked, endemic in Southern China/SE Asia, younger patients, RADIOSENSITIVE.
Risk factors
Epstein-Barr virus, Southern Chinese/SE Asian ethnicity, salted-fish diet.
Commonest presentation
Neck lump (nodal spread).
High-yield red flag
Persistent UNILATERAL middle-ear effusion (serous otitis media) in an adult = NPC until proven otherwise (Eustachian tube obstruction).
Also
Unilateral nasal obstruction/epistaxis, cranial nerve palsies (skull-base invasion), Trotter’s triad.
Investigate
Nasendoscopy + biopsy; EBV DNA/serology; MRI nasopharynx/skull base; PET-CT staging.
Treatment
RADIOTHERAPY (± chemotherapy) — radiosensitive; surgery has a limited role.
Golden rule
Don’t excise a neck node before finding the primary — investigate for an occult primary (NPC) first.
What & Why

Oral cavity lesions span a huge range — from trivial and self-limiting (aphthous ulcers, geographic tongue) to premalignant (leukoplakia, erythroplakia) to frank cancer (oral squamous cell carcinoma). The mouth is easily examinable yet oral cancer is frequently caught late. The organising question is always: is this benign, premalignant, or malignant — and does it meet 2-week-wait criteria?

The core thread: most oral cancers are squamous cell carcinomas (SCC), driven by smoking, alcohol, and betel/areca nut, and many are preceded by a visible premalignant patch (leukoplakia/erythroplakia) — so recognising and biopsying the premalignant lesion is a chance to intervene early.
The Decisive Fork — Benign vs Premalignant vs Malignant
CategoryExamplesAction
Benign / self-limitingAphthous ulcers, geographic tongue, candidiasis, gingivitis, traumatic ulcerReassure / treat cause
PremalignantLeukoplakia, erythroplakia, oral lichen planus, submucous fibrosisBiopsy — assess dysplasia
MalignantOral SCC (ulcer/mass/non-healing lesion)2WW referral + biopsy
Premalignant Lesions
⚪ Leukoplakia
  • White patches — typically asymptomatic, irregular, raised, and fixed (cannot be wiped off)
  • Premalignant → risk of oral SCC; transformation ~1% per year (higher with dysplasia, tongue/floor of mouth, size >2 cm, non-smokers, speckled/verrucous forms)
  • Definition: a white patch that cannot be characterised as any other disease (a diagnosis of exclusion — rule out candida, lichen planus, frictional keratosis)
  • Biopsy is essential to exclude dysplasia/cancer — can’t be diagnosed by appearance alone
🔴 Erythroplakia
  • Like leukoplakia but the patches are RED (or red-and-white / “speckled”) — a bright red, velvety patch that can’t be attributed to another cause
  • MUCH higher malignant potential than leukoplakia — a large proportion already show dysplasia/carcinoma-in-situ or invasive SCC on biopsy → always biopsy, low threshold to excise
Rule of thumb: red beats white for danger — a red (erythroplakia) or mixed red-white (speckled) lesion is more worrying than a pure white one.
Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
  • >90% of oral cancers are SCC; commonest sites: lateral border of the tongue, floor of mouth, lip
  • Risk factors: smoking/tobacco, alcohol (synergistic), betel quid / areca nut / paan (major in South Asian populations), HPV (more oropharyngeal), sun exposure (lip), immunosuppression, premalignant lesions, chronic irritation
  • Features: a persistent (>3 week) ulcer or mass — non-healing, indurated (firm) edges, exophytic or ulcerated, bleeding, pain, referred otalgia, loose teeth, dysphagia, a neck lump (nodal spread)
  • Investigate: biopsy (definitive) + imaging (CT/MRI/PET) for staging; assess the neck
  • Manage (H&N MDT): surgery ± radiotherapy ± chemotherapy by stage; reconstruction; SALT support
Referral — NICE NG12 (2-Week-Wait)
Consider a suspected-cancer (2WW) referral for: unexplained oral ulceration lasting >3 weeks, OR a persistent and unexplained neck lump.
  • A dentist should urgently (2WW) refer: a lump on the lip / in the oral cavity, OR a red or red-and-white patch consistent with erythroplakia / erythroleukoplakia
  • Unexplained one-sided head/neck pain >4 weeks with earache but normal otoscopy
  • An unexplained recent neck lump, or a previously undiagnosed lump that has changed over 3–6 weeks; an unexplained persistent sore/painful throat
  • Oral symptoms/signs persisting >6 weeks that can’t be definitively diagnosed as benign
Verified against NG12: the 2017 update removed the requirement that a red/red-white patch be “painful, swollen or bleeding”, and routes these via a dentist for a second opinion.
Common Benign Conditions (the “not cancer” differentials)
🦷 Gingival / gum conditions
  • Gingival hyperplasia (gum overgrowth) — causes: gingivitis, pregnancy, vitamin C deficiency (scurvy), acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), and drugs — calcium-channel blockers (CCB), phenytoin, ciclosporin (classic drug triad)
  • Gingivitis — swollen, bleeding-on-brushing, painful gums, halitosis
  • Acute necrotising ulcerative gingivitis (ANUG) — rapid, very painful gum ulceration (anaerobic; smoking/stress/immunosuppression) → refer to dentist, oral metronidazole 3 days, chlorhexidine/hydrogen-peroxide mouthwash, analgesia
👅 Other mouth / tongue lesions
  • Aphthous ulcers — recurrent, painful shallow ulcers (grey base/red halo); self-limiting <2 wks; if severe/persistent consider iron/B12/folate deficiency, coeliac, IBD, Behçet’s. Any ulcer >3 weeks → 2WW (could be SCC)
  • Oral candidiasis (thrush) — white plaques that WIPE OFF (erythematous base) — distinguishes from leukoplakia; antifungals
  • Oral lichen planus — lacy white striae (Wickham’s) ± erosions; small premalignant potential
  • Geographic tongue — map-like migrating red patches; benign, reassure
  • Glossitis — smooth, red, sore tongue → iron, B12, folate deficiency; black hairy tongue — benign (hygiene/smoking)
Exam Pearls
Three categories
Benign (aphthous ulcer, candidiasis, geographic tongue) vs premalignant (leukoplakia, erythroplakia) vs malignant (oral SCC).
Leukoplakia
White patch that CANNOT be wiped off (vs candida, which wipes off), premalignant → BIOPSY.
Erythroplakia
Red/speckled patch, MUCH higher malignant potential than leukoplakia → biopsy + excise. “Red beats white for danger.”
Oral SCC
>90% of oral cancer; tongue/floor of mouth/lip; smoking + alcohol + betel quid; non-healing indurated ulcer/mass; refer + biopsy.
2WW
Unexplained oral ulcer >3 weeks or persistent neck lump; red/red-white patch or lip/oral lump → urgent dentist; lesion >6 weeks.
Golden rule
ANY oral ulcer lasting >3 weeks = cancer until proven otherwise.
Gingival hyperplasia
Drug causes: CCBs, phenytoin, ciclosporin (+ pregnancy, scurvy, AML).
ANUG
→ dentist + oral metronidazole + chlorhexidine mouthwash + analgesia.
Glossitis
Smooth red sore tongue → iron/B12/folate deficiency.
Key bedside distinction
Candida wipes off; leukoplakia doesn’t.
What & Why

“Head and neck cancer” covers malignancies of the oral cavity, pharynx (naso-/oro-/hypopharynx), larynx, salivary glands, thyroid, and nasal cavity/sinuses. The vast majority (outside thyroid) are squamous cell carcinomas (SCC) driven by smoking, alcohol, betel/areca nut, and HPV. This is the synthesis topic: H&N cancers present with vague, overlapping, “innocent” symptoms (a hoarse voice, a sore throat, a neck lump, an ear that won’t clear) — most benign — so the vital skill is a single, reliable red-flag / referral framework to catch the few cancers early.

The organising principle: almost every red flag reduces to “unexplained + persistent (usually ≥3 weeks) + in an at-risk person”. Persistence and lack of an obvious benign explanation are what turn a common symptom into a referral.
The Unifying Red Flags (NICE NG12) — by Site
SiteConsider 2WW referral if…
LaryngealAged ≥45 with persistent unexplained hoarseness OR an unexplained neck lump
OralUnexplained oral ulceration lasting >3 weeks, OR a persistent unexplained neck lump
Oral (→ dentist, urgent)A lump on the lip / in the oral cavity, OR a red or red-and-white patch (erythroplakia/erythroleukoplakia)
ThyroidAn unexplained thyroid lump
The Practical Red-Flag List

Refer / have a low threshold for any of these, especially in a smoker/drinker:

  • Persistent hoarseness >3 weeks
  • Dysphagia (or odynophagia) >3 weeks
  • Persistent unexplained neck lump / lymphadenopathy (or a known lump that changes over 3–6 weeks)
  • Unexplained oral ulcer or swelling >3 weeks
  • Red, or red-and-white, oral patches
  • Persistent unilateral sore throat (especially with a “lump in throat” sensation)
  • Persistent unilateral otalgia with a NORMAL otoscopy (>4 weeks) — referred pain from a pharyngeal/laryngeal tumour (a classic trap)
  • Persistent unilateral nasal obstruction / epistaxis (→ nasopharyngeal/sinonasal tumour)
  • Blood in the mouth / haemoptysis with a lump-in-throat sensation; any oral sign/symptom >6 weeks not confidently benign
The three “persistent >3 weeks” oral red flags to memorise: (1) a head/neck lump, (2) an oral ulcer/swelling, (3) a red or mixed red-white oral patch.
Emergency (not 2WW): stridor → same-day / emergency ENT + airway management.
Risk Factors (who to worry about)
  • Smoking / tobacco (dominant across sites); alcohol (synergistic)
  • Betel quid / areca nut / paan (oral cancer — South/Southeast Asian populations)
  • HPV (oropharyngeal — rising incidence, better prognosis); EBV (nasopharyngeal — Southern Chinese/SE Asian)
  • Sun exposure (lip), occupational (wood dust/formaldehyde → sinonasal; asbestos)
  • Premalignant lesions (leukoplakia, erythroplakia), immunosuppression, previous H&N cancer/radiotherapy, poor oral hygiene
The Neck Lump — a Special Note
A persistent unexplained neck lump is one of the commonest presentations of head & neck cancer (nodal metastasis).
  • In an adult (>45), a firm, non-tender, persistent cervical node is malignancy until proven otherwise (metastatic SCC, lymphoma, thyroid)
  • Find the primary before biopsying the node — do NOT do an open/excisional lymph node biopsy first (risks tumour seeding + complicates later surgery); investigate with nasendoscopy + FNA/core biopsy + imaging
  • Ultrasound-guided FNA is the standard first tissue diagnosis for a neck node
  • Consider an unknown-primary SCC (metastatic node with occult primary — often tonsil/base of tongue; investigate with PET-CT, tonsillectomy, HPV/EBV testing)
The Diagnostic Pathway (once referred)
  • Flexible nasendoscopy — examine the whole upper aerodigestive tract (nasopharynx → larynx)
  • Biopsy — of the primary (panendoscopy/EUA + biopsy) for histology; FNA for neck nodes
  • Imaging: CT/MRI of the neck (+ thorax) for local/nodal staging; PET-CT for distant disease/unknown primary
  • HPV (p16) testing (oropharyngeal), EBV (nasopharyngeal)
  • MDT staging (TNM) → determines treatment (surgery / radiotherapy / chemoradiotherapy, by site & stage)
Safety-Netting (the primary-care reality)
Many H&N symptoms are benign (e.g. laryngopharyngeal reflux is a very common cause of “throat symptoms” and a frequent 2WW outcome) — but because they overlap with cancer, the rule is: treat the presumed benign cause AND safety-net (e.g. a PPI trial for reflux with clear “return if not resolving/worsening” advice), and refer if it persists.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Mostly SCC (oral/pharynx/larynx); risk factors: smoking, alcohol, betel quid, HPV (oropharynx), EBV (nasopharynx).
Red-flag principle
“Unexplained + persistent ≥3 weeks + at-risk person.”
Laryngeal 2WW
≥45 + persistent hoarseness OR neck lump.
Oral 2WW
Oral ulcer >3 weeks OR persistent neck lump; red/red-white patch or lip/oral lump → urgent dentist.
Thyroid 2WW
Unexplained thyroid lump.
Classic trap
Persistent unilateral otalgia + NORMAL otoscopy = referred pain from a pharyngeal/laryngeal tumour.
Neck lump
Commonest H&N cancer presentation; find the primary before excising the node (FNA, nasendoscopy, imaging).
Emergency
Stridor → EMERGENCY (same-day), not 2WW.
Pathway
Nasendoscopy → biopsy/FNA → CT/MRI/PET staging → MDT.
Safety-net
Treat benign-looking throat symptoms (e.g. LPR/PPI trial) and refer if persistent.
ENT__Neck Lumps & Salivary Gland Disease:
Overview — neck lumps & salivary gland disease
Neck swellings and salivary gland pathology — a common surgical presentation where age, site and history narrow the differential.
The organising principle: by age & site. Congenital (branchial cyst — lateral; thyroglossal — midline, moves with tongue protrusion; dermoid), inflammatory (reactive nodes), and neoplastic (lymphoma, metastatic SCC, salivary tumours). A persistent adult neck lump is cancer until proven otherwise.
ConditionClue
Neck lumps (branchial/thyroglossal/dermoid)branchial = lateral, young adult; thyroglossal = midline, moves with tongue protrusion; dermoid = midline
Salivary gland pathologystones (meal-related swelling), sialadenitis, tumours (pleomorphic adenoma commonest — parotid; malignant if facial nerve involved)
A persistent neck lump in an adult (esp. >45, smoker) is malignant until proven otherwise → 2-week-wait + imaging/FNA (not excision biopsy first). Facial nerve palsy with a parotid mass suggests malignancy.
What & Why

A neck lump has a broad differential spanning congenital, infective/inflammatory, and neoplastic causes. The same finding can be a trivial reactive node or the first sign of a head-and-neck cancer or lymphoma — so the skill is a structured approach using age, location (midline vs lateral), and characteristics, always keeping the red flags for malignancy in mind.

The core triage logic: reactive lymphadenopathy is the commonest cause overall. In children/young adults, lumps are usually congenital or inflammatory. In adults >40 with a persistent lump, assume malignancy (metastatic squamous cell carcinoma or lymphoma) until proven otherwise.
The First Fork — Age & Location
MidlineLateral
CongenitalThyroglossal cyst, dermoid cystBranchial cyst, cystic hygroma
ThyroidThyroid nodule/goitre (moves on swallowing)—
Nodes/other—Reactive/malignant lymphadenopathy, carotid body tumour, pharyngeal pouch
The Congenital Cysts
💧 Thyroglossal cyst
  • Commonest congenital midline neck cyst — a persisting thyroglossal duct (the track the thyroid leaves descending from the foramen caecum at the tongue base)
  • Midline, mobile, non-tender, soft, fluctuant
  • Moves upwards on tongue protrusion (and swallowing) — the classic sign. OSCE gold: ask the patient to stick their tongue out
  • Ix: USS/CT; check thyroid function/imaging (the cyst may contain the only functioning thyroid)
  • Mx: Sistrunk procedure (excises cyst + central hyoid + duct tract to prevent recurrence)
💧 Branchial cyst
  • Lateral cyst: oval, mobile, non-tender, cystic, anterior to sternocleidomastoid (SCM), near the angle of the mandible
  • Failure of obliteration of the 2nd branchial cleft; presents in teens/early adulthood; may enlarge/infect
  • Aspirate shows cholesterol crystals — hook: branCHial = CHolesterol
  • In an adult >40, a “branchial cyst” may be a cystic metastasis from a head-and-neck SCC — do USS-guided FNA before excision
  • Mx: surgical excision
💧 Dermoid cyst
  • A midline cyst from ectodermal tissue trapped during embryonic fusion — contains skin appendages (keratin, hair, sebaceous material)
  • Typically midline (submental / floor of mouth), soft, non-tender; can mimic a thyroglossal cyst — but a dermoid does NOT move with tongue protrusion (key distinguisher)
  • Mx: surgical excision
The Other Neck Lumps
LumpKey features
Reactive lymphadenopathyCommonest cause; recent local/viral infection; tender, mobile, settles in 2–6 weeks
LymphomaRubbery, painless nodes; B symptoms (night sweats, fever, weight loss); may be generalised
Cystic hygromaCongenital lymphatic malformation, classically left neck; ~90% by age 2; transilluminates — hook: cystic hyGLOWma
Carotid body tumourPulsatile lateral mass; moves side-to-side but NOT vertically; no movement on swallowing; a bruit may be present
Pharyngeal pouch (Zenker’s)Older men; herniation at Killian’s dehiscence (between thyropharyngeus + cricopharyngeus); gurgles on palpation; dysphagia, regurgitation, aspiration, chronic cough
LipomaSoft, non-tender, mobile, no skin changes; benign fat tumour; reassure
Thyroid nodule/goitreMidline/paramedian; moves up on swallowing (not on tongue protrusion — distinguishes from thyroglossal cyst)
Two “movement” signs to nail: moves with tongue protrusion → thyroglossal cyst; moves with swallowing (but not tongue protrusion) → thyroid.
Red Flags for Malignancy
  • Persistent lump >3 weeks in an adult (especially >45)
  • Hard, fixed, non-tender node
  • Associated: hoarseness/voice change, dysphagia, odynophagia, referred otalgia, unexplained weight loss, a mouth/throat ulcer
  • Risk factors: smoking, alcohol, betel nut, HPV (oropharyngeal)
  • Unexplained neck lump in an adult → urgent (2-week-wait) suspected head-and-neck cancer referral (NICE NG12)
Investigations
  • History + examination (age, duration, location, characteristics, red flags, full ENT exam of mouth/throat/nose)
  • Ultrasound — first-line imaging (cystic vs solid, nodes, thyroid)
  • Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) — usually USS-guided; key for solid/suspicious lumps. If lymphoma is suspected → core or excisional biopsy (FNA can’t subtype lymphoma — needs architecture)
  • CT/MRI for staging if malignancy suspected; nasendoscopy/panendoscopy to find a primary if metastatic SCC suspected
  • Bloods (FBC, ± viral serology, LDH if lymphoma; thyroid function for thyroid lesions)
Exam Pearls
Commonest
Reactive lymphadenopathy. Children → congenital/inflammatory; adults >40 with persistent lump → cancer until proven otherwise.
Midline
Thyroglossal cyst (moves with tongue protrusion), dermoid (doesn’t move with tongue), thyroid (moves with swallowing).
Lateral
Branchial cyst (anterior to SCM, teens, “branCHial = CHolesterol”), cystic hygroma (transilluminates, “hyGLOWma”), carotid body tumour (pulsatile, side-to-side only).
Thyroglossal
→ Sistrunk procedure.
Adult branchial
A “branchial cyst” in an adult >40 may be cystic SCC metastasis → FNA before excision.
Lymphoma
Rubbery painless nodes + B symptoms → core/excisional biopsy (NOT FNA).
Pharyngeal pouch
Older man, gurgling midline lump, dysphagia/regurgitation.
Red flag
Persistent unexplained neck lump in an adult → 2-week-wait head & neck cancer referral.
Investigation
USS → FNAC (core biopsy if lymphoma).
What & Why

Salivary gland disease covers inflammation, obstruction (stones), and tumours. It matters because the anatomy predicts the pathology (tumours favour the parotid, stones the submandibular), and because the crucial skill is spotting the red flags for malignancy — especially facial nerve involvement, since the facial nerve runs through the parotid. The backbone: the “rule of 80s” and the benign-tumour duo (pleomorphic adenoma + Warthin’s).

Anatomy — the Three Gland Pairs
GlandLocationPredominant pathology
ParotidAnterior + inferior to the earMost tumours (but most parotid tumours are benign)
SubmandibularBelow the angle of the jawMost stones (~80%)
SublingualBeneath the tongueMucous (rare tumours, but higher % malignant)
The facial nerve (CN VII) passes through the parotid gland, dividing it into superficial + deep lobes — why parotid surgery risks facial nerve damage, and why facial nerve palsy with a parotid lump = malignancy until proven otherwise.
The “Rule of 80s”
  • ~80% of salivary tumours are in the parotid
  • ~80% of parotid tumours are benign
  • ~80% of benign parotid tumours are pleomorphic adenomas
  • The smaller the gland, the higher the proportion malignant (sublingual/minor-gland tumours are more often cancer)
The Decisive Fork — Tumour vs Obstruction vs Inflammation
TumourStone / obstructionSialadenitis
StoryPersistent, painless lumpPain + swelling worse on eatingPainful, swollen, often unwell
OnsetSlow (benign) or rapid (malignant)Recurrent, mealtime-relatedAcute
Key clueFacial nerve palsy → malignantPalpable stone; submandibularPurulent discharge from duct
Salivary Gland Tumours
🟦 Pleomorphic adenoma
  • Commonest salivary gland tumour; typically 40–60 years
  • Slow-growing, painless, mobile parotid lump
  • Mx: surgical excision (superficial parotidectomy) — risk of facial nerve (CN VII) damage
  • Do NOT enucleate (→ recurrence); small risk of malignant transformation → carcinoma ex-pleomorphic adenoma
🟩 Warthin’s tumour
  • Benign, the 2nd commonest benign tumour (adenolymphoma)
  • Middle-aged males, strongly linked to smoking; almost exclusively parotid; can be bilateral
  • Softer, more mobile, fluctuant/cystic (vs the firmer pleomorphic adenoma)
🔴 Malignant tumours
  • Mucoepidermoid carcinoma — the commonest salivary malignancy (esp. parotid)
  • Adenoid cystic carcinoma — notorious for perineural invasion (pain, facial nerve involvement) + late distant spread
  • Others: acinic cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, carcinoma ex-pleomorphic adenoma
  • Red flags: rapid growth, pain, hard/fixed lump, facial nerve palsy, cervical lymphadenopathy, skin fixation/ulceration
Salivary Gland Stones (Sialolithiasis)
  • Recurrent unilateral pain + swelling on eating (saliva is stimulated but can’t drain past the stone)
  • ~80% are submandibular — Wharton’s duct runs uphill + its saliva is thick/mucinous → prone to stones
  • May become infected → sialadenitis, and rarely spread (Ludwig’s angina — floor-of-mouth cellulitis, an airway emergency)
  • Ix: plain X-ray, sialography, ultrasound; non-contrast CT is sensitive
  • Mx: conservative (hydration, sialogogues e.g. lemon/sour sweets, gland massage, warm compresses); stone removal (endoscopic sialendoscopy or surgery); gland excision if recurrent
Sialadenitis
  • Inflammation/infection of a salivary gland, often secondary to obstruction by a stone
  • Purulent discharge from the duct → foul taste in the mouth
  • Acute bacterial (commonly Staph aureus; ascending from the mouth — often in dehydrated/elderly patients) → tender, swollen, erythematous gland ± pus at the duct
  • Viral: mumps — bilateral parotid swelling
  • Chronic/autoimmune: recurrent — think Sjögren’s syndrome (dry eyes/mouth) and IgG4-related disease
  • Mx: hydration, analgesia, oral hygiene, antibiotics for bacterial infection; treat the underlying obstruction; drain any abscess
Investigations (general)
  • Ultrasound — first-line (cystic vs solid, stones, gland structure)
  • Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) — for tumours (± US-guided)
  • MRI — best soft-tissue characterisation + staging (deep lobe, perineural spread)
  • Sialography / CT for stones; bloods (autoimmune screen if Sjögren’s suspected)
Exam Pearls
Anatomy predicts pathology
Parotid = most TUMOURS; submandibular = most STONES (~80%); minor glands = higher % malignant.
Rule of 80s
80% of tumours parotid; 80% of parotid tumours benign; 80% of those pleomorphic adenomas.
Pleomorphic adenoma
Commonest, 40–60y, slow painless mobile parotid lump → superficial parotidectomy (risk CN VII). Don’t enucleate.
Warthin’s
Benign, older male smokers, can be bilateral, softer/cystic.
Malignancy
Commonest = mucoepidermoid carcinoma; adenoid cystic = perineural invasion.
Red flag
Facial nerve palsy + parotid lump = malignant until proven otherwise. Also: rapid growth, pain, fixed/hard, lymphadenopathy.
Stones
Recurrent unilateral pain/swelling ON EATING; ~80% submandibular; XR/sialography; can → sialadenitis/Ludwig’s angina.
Sialadenitis
Obstruction → infection, purulent duct discharge/foul taste; Staph (bacterial), mumps (viral), Sjögren’s (autoimmune).
Investigation
Tumour: USS + FNAC (± MRI).
ENT__Cholesteatoma:
What & Why

A cholesteatoma is an abnormal collection of keratinising squamous epithelium (skin) in the middle ear and mastoid — essentially “skin growing where it shouldn’t be” behind the eardrum. Despite being benign (not a cancer, despite the “-oma”), it is locally destructive: it erodes bone as it expands → eats through the ossicles, mastoid, facial nerve canal, inner ear, even the skull base → hearing loss, facial palsy, vertigo, and life-threatening intracranial complications. The classic “unsafe” chronic ear disease.

The name is a misnomer — it contains neither cholesterol (“chole”) nor fat (“steat”); it’s keratinising squamous epithelium + keratin debris.
The Core Mechanism
📷 Image placeholder — Stepwise mechanism — Eustachian tube dysfunction → negative middle-ear pressure → pars flaccida retraction pocket → trapped keratin → an expanding, bone-eroding sac
1
Eustachian tube dysfunction→ negative pressure in the middle ear
↓
2
Retraction pocketthe weak pars flaccida / attic is sucked inward
↓
3
Trapped keratinthe pocket can no longer self-clean → desquamated skin/keratin accumulates into an expanding sac
↓
4
Bone destructionthe sac releases bone-destroying enzymes + gets repeatedly infected → erodes surrounding structures
This explains why it forms at the attic (pars flaccida), why it produces foul discharge (trapped, infected keratin), and why it destroys bone.
Types
Acquired (commonest)
  • Primary acquired — from a retraction pocket (the mechanism above), usually pars flaccida/attic in adults
  • Secondary acquired — from direct injury/perforation of the eardrum (infection/trauma)
Congenital
  • A pearly white mass behind an intact eardrum in a child, no history of discharge/perforation (a rest of embryonic epithelium)
Clinical Features
  • Foul-smelling ear discharge (otorrhoea) — persistent, often not resolving with antibiotics
  • Unilateral conductive hearing loss (ossicular erosion)
  • May also have ear fullness/discomfort
“Danger” features (expansion into surrounding structures): infection, pain; vertigo (erosion into the labyrinth/semicircular canals — a fistula; classically vertigo on pressing the tragus); facial nerve palsy (erosion of the facial canal); tinnitus, sensorineural loss.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Otoscopy of an attic (pars flaccida) cholesteatoma — a pearly-white keratin mass/crust in the upper drum with a retraction pocket (the key bedside sign); HRCT temporal bone maps ossicular/scutum erosion before surgery
  • Otoscopy — the key bedside finding: an abnormal build-up of whitish/pearly debris or crust in the upper (attic) part of the eardrum (pars flaccida), ± a retraction pocket or perforation
  • Any crusting/wax obscuring the attic (pars flaccida) is a cholesteatoma until proven otherwise — needs proper examination/microsuction to see behind it
  • High-resolution CT of the temporal bone — confirms the diagnosis, maps its extent, + assesses bony erosion (ossicles, mastoid, facial canal, tegmen) before surgery
  • Audiometry — documents the (usually conductive) hearing loss
  • Diffusion-weighted MRI — for detecting residual/recurrent cholesteatoma after surgery
Management
Definitive treatment = surgical removal — a cholesteatoma does NOT resolve with antibiotics or “watching”; it must be excised. Refer urgently to ENT.
🔪 Surgery
  • Mastoidectomy ± tympanoplasty — removes the cholesteatoma from the mastoid/middle ear + reconstructs the eardrum/hearing where possible
  • Canal-wall-up (preserves canal anatomy, higher recurrence) vs canal-wall-down (open mastoid cavity, lower recurrence) depending on extent
💊 Adjuncts / follow-up
  • Topical antibiotics + aural toilet (microsuction) — control active infection/discharge peri-operatively, but not curative
  • Long-term follow-up — high recurrence/residual rate (~20–30%) → surveillance (clinical ± DWI-MRI)
Complications (why it’s “unsafe”)
📷 Image placeholder — Erosion targets — ossicles (conductive loss), facial-nerve canal (palsy), lateral semicircular canal (fistula/vertigo) and tegmen (intracranial spread)
  • Local: conductive (± sensorineural) hearing loss, ossicular erosion, facial nerve palsy, labyrinthine fistula → vertigo/SNHL
  • Extracranial: mastoiditis, petrositis
  • Intracranial (life-threatening): meningitis, brain abscess, sigmoid/lateral sinus thrombosis
Exam Pearls
What it is
Keratinising squamous epithelium (skin) in the middle ear/mastoid — benign but LOCALLY DESTRUCTIVE (erodes bone). Name is a misnomer (no cholesterol/fat).
Mechanism
Eustachian tube dysfunction → negative pressure → pars flaccida (attic) retraction pocket → trapped keratin → expanding, bone-eroding sac.
Presentation
Foul-smelling ear discharge + unilateral CONDUCTIVE hearing loss + attic crust/debris on otoscopy.
Clinical rule
“Crusting/wax obscuring the attic (pars flaccida) = cholesteatoma until proven otherwise.”
Danger signs
Vertigo (labyrinthine fistula — worse on pressing tragus), facial nerve palsy, pain.
Investigations
CT temporal bone confirms + maps extent; audiometry; DWI-MRI for recurrence.
Treatment
Definitive = SURGERY (mastoidectomy ± tympanoplasty) — antibiotics don’t cure it.
Complications
Facial palsy, labyrinthine fistula, mastoiditis, and life-threatening MENINGITIS / BRAIN ABSCESS / sinus thrombosis.
Congenital
Pearly white mass behind an INTACT drum in a child, no discharge.
ENT__Epistaxis Management:
What & Why

Epistaxis is bleeding from the nose — one of the commonest ENT emergencies (~60% have one in their lifetime). Most are trivial and self-limiting, but a minority — especially posterior bleeds in older, anticoagulated patients — are profuse, risk airway compromise + haemodynamic instability. The essence: the anterior vs posterior distinction, the stepwise management ladder (first aid → cautery → packing → surgery), and the contributing factors (anticoagulation, hypertension).

The core anatomy: most bleeds come from Little’s area on the anterior nasal septum, the site of Kiesselbach’s plexus — an anastomosis of branches from both the internal + external carotid systems (sphenopalatine, anterior/posterior ethmoidal, greater palatine, superior labial arteries). Because it’s superficial + exposed, it bleeds easily → ~90% of epistaxis is anterior.
The Decisive Fork — Anterior vs Posterior

  • Bleeding disorders — haemophilia, thrombocytopenia, liver disease
  • Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT / Osler-Weber-Rendu) — recurrent bleeds + mucocutaneous telangiectasia
  • Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) — vasculitis, crusting/septal perforation
  • Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma — a vascular tumour in adolescent boys → recurrent unilateral epistaxis + nasal obstruction (a can’t-miss cause); idiopathic (common)

ENT__Hearing Assessment (Weber & Rinne):
What & Why

Weber’s and Rinne’s are bedside tuning-fork tests that distinguish conductive from sensorineural hearing loss. This single distinction is the first fork in the road for every ear complaint — it points to completely different causes and management (a wax plug / glue ear / otosclerosis vs a cochlear/nerve problem), and it’s guaranteed OSCE and written-exam material. Quick, cheap, no kit beyond a tuning fork — but screening tests, not a replacement for formal audiometry.

The core physiology: Air conduction (AC) = sound → ear canal → eardrum → ossicles → cochlea (the normal, amplified route — the outer/middle ear add gain). Bone conduction (BC) = the fork on the skull vibrates the cochlea directly, bypassing the outer/middle ear. In a normal ear, AC > BC (the middle ear amplifies, so the air route wins).
🔇 Conductive loss (outer/middle ear)
  • The AC pathway is blocked → BC now beats AC in that ear
🔉 Sensorineural loss (cochlea/nerve)
  • Both AC and BC are reduced equally → AC still > BC (the ratio is preserved, but everything is quieter)
Relevant Anatomy
  • The inner ear contains the bony labyrinth (fluid-filled: perilymph and endolymph) — three parts: semicircular canals, vestibule, and cochlea
  • Balance (vestibular): the semicircular canals detect head rotation; the otolith organs (utricle & saccule) in the vestibule detect gravity + linear acceleration
  • Hearing: the cochlea
  • The vestibular nerve (balance) + cochlear nerve (hearing) form the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) — why VIII lesions (e.g. acoustic neuroma) cause both sensorineural loss and imbalance
The Decisive Fork — Conductive vs Sensorineural
Conductive (CHL)Sensorineural (SNHL)
ProblemOuter/middle ear (sound can’t get in)Cochlea or CN VIII (sound isn’t processed)
CausesWax, otitis media/glue ear, perforation, otosclerosis, cholesteatomaPresbycusis, noise, ototoxic drugs, Ménière’s, acoustic neuroma, congenital
Rinne (affected ear)NEGATIVE (BC > AC)POSITIVE (AC > BC) — normal pattern
WeberLateralises to the AFFECTED earLateralises to the UNAFFECTED (better) ear
Rinne’s Test
📷 Image placeholder — Rinne technique — 512 Hz fork base on the mastoid (bone conduction) then tines at the ear canal (air conduction); positive = AC>BC (normal/SNHL), negative = BC>AC (conductive)

Tests AC vs BC in each ear.

  • Method: strike a 512 Hz tuning fork; place the base on the mastoid process (BC). When the patient can no longer hear it, move the tines next to the ear canal (AC). Ask which is louder / whether they hear it again in the air
  • Rinne POSITIVE = AC > BC = NORMAL (or sensorineural loss)
  • Rinne NEGATIVE = BC > AC = CONDUCTIVE loss in that ear
  • Why 512 Hz? Optimal balance — lower forks (128/256 Hz) are felt as vibration (false results); higher forks decay too fast
Memory aid: “Rinne positive = normal; a negative Rinne (BC beats AC) means sound can’t get through the conducting apparatus → conductive.” (Note the confusing naming: “negative” = abnormal/conductive.)
Weber’s Test
📷 Image placeholder — Weber test — forehead-midline fork; lateralises TO the affected ear in conductive loss and AWAY to the better ear in sensorineural loss

Tests for asymmetry — lateralisation.

  • Method: strike the 512 Hz fork; place the base in the midline — on the forehead/vertex. Ask: “Where do you hear it — middle, or louder on one side?”
  • Normal (or symmetrical loss): heard equally / in the midline
  • Conductive loss → lateralises to the AFFECTED (worse) ear — the blocked ear is shielded from background/masking noise, so bone-conducted sound seems louder there
  • Sensorineural loss → lateralises to the UNAFFECTED (better) ear — the damaged cochlea/nerve can’t detect it, so the good ear wins
Memory aid: “Weber → Conductive goes to the Crap (affected) ear; Sensorineural goes to the Sound (good) ear.”
Putting Them Together (the classic patterns)
📷 Image placeholder — Summary grid — Normal, Left conductive and Left sensorineural rows showing the paired Rinne (which ear positive/negative) and Weber (central/left/right) findings
FindingRinneWeber
NormalPositive both ears (AC>BC)Central/equal
Left CHLNegative left (BC>AC), positive rightLateralises LEFT (affected)
Left SNHLPositive both earsLateralises RIGHT (unaffected)
Pitfall — the “False-Negative Rinne”
In a severe/total unilateral SNHL (a “dead ear”), placing the fork on the affected mastoid → the sound crosses the skull and is heard by the opposite (normal) cochlea via bone conduction → the patient reports “BC > AC” on the dead side → a falsely NEGATIVE Rinne (mimicking conductive loss).
  • Weber resolves it: it will lateralise to the good ear (confirming SNHL, not CHL) — exactly why the two tests are done together
  • Masking (a Barany noise box in the good ear) can also confirm
Beyond the Bedside
  • Pure-tone audiometry (PTA) — the definitive hearing test; plots AC (headphones) and BC (mastoid) thresholds across frequencies. An air–bone gap = conductive component; both lines depressed together = sensorineural
  • Tympanometry — middle-ear function/compliance (e.g. flat “type B” trace in glue ear)
  • Otoacoustic emissions / auditory brainstem response — newborn screening, retrocochlear assessment
  • Tuning-fork tests only reliably detect a conductive loss of ~≥30 dB and are best for pure unilateral losses; bilateral/mixed → PTA
Exam Pearls
Normal ear
AC > BC (air conduction wins — the middle ear amplifies).
Rinne
POSITIVE = AC>BC = normal/SNHL; NEGATIVE = BC>AC = CONDUCTIVE. (Confusingly, “negative” = abnormal.)
Weber
Lateralises to the AFFECTED ear in conductive loss; to the UNAFFECTED (better) ear in sensorineural loss.
Fork
Use a 512 Hz fork (lower = felt as vibration; higher = decays too fast).
False-negative Rinne
In a “dead ear” (severe SNHL) sound crosses to the good side → Weber (to good ear) confirms it’s really SNHL.
Causes
Conductive: wax, glue ear/otitis media, perforation, otosclerosis, cholesteatoma. SNHL: presbycusis, noise, ototoxic drugs, Ménière’s, acoustic neuroma.
CN VIII
= cochlear (hearing) + vestibular (balance) → VIII lesions cause both (e.g. acoustic neuroma).
Definitive test
Pure-tone audiometry (air–bone gap = conductive); tympanometry for the middle ear.
ENT__Ramsay Hunt Syndrome:
What & Why

Ramsay Hunt syndrome (RHS) is a facial nerve palsy caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve, producing the triad of ear pain, a vesicular rash, and lower-motor-neuron facial weakness. It’s the second commonest cause of atraumatic facial palsy (after Bell’s palsy), has a worse prognosis than Bell’s, and early antiviral + steroid treatment (within 72 hours) substantially improves recovery — a time-critical “treat now, don’t wait” diagnosis. Core: facial palsy + vesicles around the ear = Ramsay Hunt (not Bell’s) → aciclovir + steroids.

The core mechanism: after chickenpox, VZV lies dormant in sensory ganglia. It reactivates in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve (CN VII) → inflammation + oedema of the nerve in its bony canal → LMN facial weakness, plus a vesicular zoster rash in the nerve’s sensory territory (the ear). Because CN VIII runs alongside CN VII in the internal acoustic meatus, it’s often affected too → vertigo, tinnitus, hearing loss.
The Decisive Fork — Ramsay Hunt vs Bell’s Palsy

Both cause LMN facial palsy (forehead involved) — the distinguishing feature is the rash and associated symptoms:

Ramsay Hunt syndromeBell’s palsy
CauseVZV reactivation (geniculate ganglion)Idiopathic (?HSV)
RashVesicular rash (ear/canal/palate)None
PainSevere otalgia (often precedes rash)Mild/none
CN VIII symptomsVertigo, tinnitus, hearing loss (common)Uncommon
PrognosisWorse (lower full-recovery rate)Better
TreatmentAntiviral + steroidSteroid (± antiviral)
Both are LOWER motor neuron palsies → the forehead IS affected (can’t wrinkle the forehead/raise the eyebrow on the affected side). An UPPER motor neuron lesion (e.g. stroke) spares the forehead — a key distinction.
Clinical Features
  • Auricular pain (otalgia) — often the first symptom, may precede the rash
  • Facial nerve palsy — unilateral LMN weakness (drooping mouth, can’t close the eye, loss of forehead wrinkling on that side)
  • Vesicular rash — around the ear (pinna, external auditory canal), may involve the tympanic membrane, palate, or anterior tongue
  • Vertigo and tinnitus (± sensorineural hearing loss) — from CN VIII involvement
  • May also have loss of taste (anterior 2/3 tongue), reduced lacrimation/dry eye, hyperacusis (branches of CN VII)
  • The rash may sometimes follow or be absent (“zoster sine herpete”) — facial palsy can precede visible vesicles
Investigations
  • Primarily a clinical diagnosis (facial palsy + vesicular rash in the ear)
  • VZV PCR (from vesicle swab/ear exudate) can confirm — useful to distinguish zoster sine herpete from Bell’s palsy
  • MRI if atypical, polycranial, or diagnostic doubt (exclude other causes)
  • Pure-tone audiometry if hearing affected
Management
Start treatment as early as possible — ideally within 72 hours of symptom onset (recovery rates are much higher with early treatment).
  • Antiviral: oral aciclovir (e.g. 800 mg five times daily for 7 days; or valaciclovir/famciclovir)
  • Corticosteroids: oral prednisolone — added to reduce nerve inflammation/oedema
  • Eye protection — if the eye won’t close, protect the cornea (lubricating drops, ointment at night, taping the eye closed) to prevent exposure keratopathy/corneal ulceration
  • Analgesia (neuropathic pain often significant); antiemetics/vestibular sedatives for vertigo
  • Treat any post-herpetic neuralgia (amitriptyline/gabapentin)
Prognosis
  • Worse than Bell’s palsy — complete recovery is less likely, especially if treatment is delayed beyond 72 hours or the initial palsy is severe (higher House-Brackmann grade)
  • Possible sequelae: incomplete facial recovery, synkinesis (involuntary co-movement), persistent hearing loss/tinnitus/vertigo
Exam Pearls
What it is
VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of CN VII → facial palsy + vesicular ear rash + otalgia.
Distinguishing feature
The VESICULAR RASH (ear/canal/palate) + severe ear pain + vertigo/tinnitus/hearing loss (CN VIII) — vs Bell’s palsy.
LMN sign
LMN palsy → forehead INVOLVED (vs UMN/stroke = forehead spared).
Treatment
Treat within 72 hours: oral aciclovir (800 mg 5×/day, 7 days) + prednisolone.
Eye care
Lubricants, tape shut if incomplete eye closure — prevent corneal damage.
Prognosis
Worse than Bell’s palsy (lower full-recovery rate); may leave synkinesis/hearing loss.
Sine herpete
Can occur as “zoster sine herpete” (palsy before/without visible vesicles) — VZV PCR helps.
ENT__Tonsillitis / Quinsy:
What & Why

Tonsillitis is acute inflammation of the tonsils (usually the palatine tonsils) — one of the commonest causes of a sore throat. Although most cases are viral and self-limiting, a minority are bacterial (Group A Strep) and carry risks of suppurative complications (quinsy) and non-suppurative sequelae (rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis). It’s a major antibiotic-stewardship topic — the Centor and FeverPAIN scores exist precisely to decide who needs antibiotics. Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) is the key suppurative complication — pus beside the tonsil, an ENT emergency.

A · Tonsillitis — Causes & Features
🦠 Causes
  • Mostly viral (adenovirus, rhinovirus, EBV, etc.)
  • Bacterial: Group A Streptococcus (Strep pyogenes) — the important one (→ penicillin V); also Strep pneumoniae
  • Palatine tonsils usually infected
  • Consider infectious mononucleosis (EBV) — exudative tonsillitis + generalised lymphadenopathy + splenomegaly (vs bacterial = anterior cervical nodes only); amoxicillin causes a rash in EBV
🩺 Clinical features
  • Sore throat, pain on swallowing (odynophagia), fever
  • Neck pain, referred ear pain, swollen tender lymph nodes
  • Exam: red, inflamed, enlarged tonsils ± exudate; anterior cervical lymphadenopathy
A · Assessment — Centor & FeverPAIN (NICE NG84)
Centor criteria
  • Predict streptococcal cause; 1 point each — antibiotics if ≥3:
  • Fever >38°C
  • Tonsillar exudate
  • Absence of cough
  • Tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy
FeverPAIN score
  • 1 point each; applies to any sore throat (tonsillitis, pharyngitis, laryngitis):
  • Fever (>38, last 24h)
  • Purulence (exudate)
  • Attend rapidly (≤3 days of onset)
  • Inflamed tonsils (severe)
  • No cough or coryza
ScoreLikelihood strep / action
FeverPAIN 0–1 / Centor 0–2Low (~13–18%) → no antibiotic, self-care + safety-net
FeverPAIN 2–3Moderate → delayed (“back-up”) prescription
FeverPAIN 4–5 / Centor 3–4High (~62%) → immediate antibiotic
A · Management
  • Consider admission if: immunocompromised, systemically unwell, dehydrated, stridor/respiratory distress, or evidence of peritonsillar abscess/cellulitis
  • Viral / low score: simple analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen), fluids; safety-net — return if not resolving after 3 days or fever >38.3
  • Antibiotics (Centor ≥3 or FeverPAIN ≥4): first-line phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) for 5–10 days
  • Penicillin allergy → clarithromycin (erythromycin in pregnancy)
  • Avoid amoxicillin (rash if EBV)
Complications: Suppurative — quinsy, otitis media, parapharyngeal/retropharyngeal abscess, Lemierre’s syndrome. Non-suppurative (post-streptococcal) — scarlet fever, rheumatic fever, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, reactive arthritis.
B · Quinsy (Peritonsillar Abscess)

A collection of pus in the peritonsillar space (between the tonsil capsule and the pharyngeal muscles) — usually a complication of (untreated) tonsillitis, but can occur alone. Mostly Strep pyogenes (Group A), often polymicrobial.

🚩 Red-flag additional signs
  • Features of tonsillitis (severe sore throat, odynophagia, fever, neck pain, referred otalgia), plus:
  • Trismus (can’t open the mouth — pterygoid irritation)
  • “Hot potato” / muffled voice (pharyngeal swelling)
  • Swelling + erythema beside the tonsil, tonsil pushed medially
  • Uvula deviated to the unaffected side; drooling, unilateral pain, halitosis
💉 Management
  • Urgent ENT review
  • Drainage — needle aspiration OR incision and drainage
  • IV antibiotics — broad-spectrum, e.g. co-amoxiclav (per local guidance)
  • Analgesia, IV fluids; a single dose of corticosteroid (dexamethasone) may reduce symptoms
  • Interval tonsillectomy may be considered after recurrent quinsy
Tonsillectomy

Performed under general anaesthesia, usually as a day case.

📋 Indications (recurrent tonsillitis — Paradise/SIGN)
  • ≥7 episodes in 1 year, OR ≥5/year for 2 years, OR ≥3/year for 3 years
  • Recurrent tonsillar abscesses (≥2 episodes of quinsy)
  • Enlarged tonsils causing obstruction — difficulty breathing/swallowing, obstructive sleep apnoea, snoring
Complications
  • Sore throat ~2 weeks, dental damage, infection, anaesthetic risks
  • Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage (can be life-threatening — aspiration risk):
  • Primary (reactionary): within 24 hours (typically the first 6–8 hours) → immediate return to theatre
  • Secondary: 5–10 days post-op, associated with wound infection → antibiotics + admit
Exam Pearls
Cause
Mostly viral; key bacterial cause = Group A Strep (S. pyogenes).
Centor
(≥3 → antibiotics): Fever >38, tonsillar Exudate, Absence of cough, tender Anterior cervical nodes.
FeverPAIN
(≥4 → antibiotics; any sore throat): Fever, Purulence, Attend ≤3 days, Inflamed tonsils, No cough/coryza.
Antibiotic
Phenoxymethylpenicillin (penicillin V) 5–10 days; clarithromycin if allergic. Avoid amoxicillin (EBV rash).
Complications
Quinsy, otitis media, scarlet/rheumatic fever, post-strep glomerulonephritis, reactive arthritis.
Quinsy
Peritonsillar abscess: TRISMUS + muffled voice + uvula deviated AWAY from the abscess → urgent ENT + drainage (aspiration/I&D) + IV co-amoxiclav.
Tonsillectomy
7/1yr, 5/yr×2, or 3/yr×3; ≥2 quinsies; obstruction/OSA.
Post-op bleed
Primary <24h (usually 6–8h) → theatre; secondary 5–10 days (infection) → antibiotics + admit.
